items.body:
South Korea's Lee says hopes reopening talks with North Korea could lead to lasting peace South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Thursday he hoped a reopening of dialogue with North Korea would lead to discussions on ending the Korean War and establishing a lasting peace, as he addressed Asia-Pacific leaders in China.
Reuters | Updated: 19-11-2026 12:55 IST | Created: 19-11-2026 12:55 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Thursday he hoped a reopening of dialogue with North Korea would lead to discussions on ending the Korean War and establishing a lasting peace, as he addressed Asia-Pacific leaders in China.
Speaking at a session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Lee said peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula were essential to shared regional prosperity and urged members to take an active interest and cooperate, according to the Korean presidential office. His statement came ahead of a trilateral summit between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States at APEC, with some analysts saying North Korea's nuclear weapons and sanctions on Pyongyang could be among the issues discussed.
South Korea's National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac told a briefing on Wednesday that Chinese President Xi Jinping told Lee at talks on the sidelines of the summit that Beijing would play a constructive role to realise peace on the Korean Peninsula. Lee also held a meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday at the summit, where they agreed to cooperate on building stable and mutually beneficial energy supply chains, according to Lee's office.

items.title: Taiwan reports two Russian military aircraft nearby, second time this week
items.summary: Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, the second time this week it has reported seeing ...
items.body:
Taiwan reports two Russian military aircraft nearby, second time this week Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, the second time this week it has reported seeing such activity.
Reuters | Updated: 19-11-2026 12:46 IST | Created: 19-11-2026 12:46 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, the second time this week it has reported seeing such activity.
The flights have come as Russian President Vladimir Putin is in China's Shenzhen for the APEC summit, where he will also hold a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. The ministry said the two Tu-95s, known by NATO as "Bears", entered Taiwan's Air Defence Identification Zone, then exited airspace around Taiwan to the island's northeast, off the port city of Keelung.
The ministry published a picture of one of the aircraft it said was taken from a Taiwanese F-16 fighter. Taiwan's armed forces used joint intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance means to monitor the full course of the activity and "responded appropriately", the ministry said in a short statement.
Taiwan said on Tuesday two Russian military aircraft had flown in a southerly direction down its east coast. Japan also reported the same activity that day and published a map showing the aircraft flying down Taiwan's east coast. An ageing Cold War-era design, some Tu-95 can carry nuclear weapons but others of that type are used for long-range surveillance and reconnaissance.
Russia's defence ministry has not responded to requests for comment. Earlier on Thursday, Taiwan's envoy to the APEC summit Stan Shih, the founder of computer maker Acer, briefly shook hands with Putin at the start of the summit.
Major semiconductor producer Taiwan has joined Western countries in placing wide economic sanctions on Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. China's military operates around Taiwan on a daily basis.
China views Taiwan as its own territory, a position Russia has repeatedly backed. Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's sovereignty claims, saying only the island's people can decide their future.

items.summary: Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said, hours before President Vladimir Putin was ...
items.body:
Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge for third time in a week ahead of US-China-Russia summit Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said, hours before President Vladimir Putin was due to meet the leaders of China and the US.
Reuters | Updated: 19-11-2026 12:43 IST | Created: 19-11-2026 12:43 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said, hours before President Vladimir Putin was due to meet the leaders of China and the US.
The timing and impact of Ukraine's attacks on the bridge, the longest in Europe and a symbol of Putin's Russia, are awkward for the Kremlin chief as he prepares to participate in what Moscow has cast as a historic trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later on Thursday. Moscow hopes the meeting will send a signal to allies and foes that it - and not the European Union and Britain - is part of an emerging new multilateral world order. In a statement on Thursday, Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the Ukrainian attack on the Black Sea peninsula, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge.
"As a result of a nighttime drone attack, train services on the railway section of the Crimean Bridge have been temporarily suspended," the ministry said in a statement on Telegram. Sergei Aksyonov, Crimea's Russian-installed governor, confirmed the attack earlier on Thursday.
The 19-kilometre (12-mile) bridge is a flagship project which Putin inaugurated in 2018 and is a symbol of Russia's attachment to the peninsula, which is also the home of its Black Sea Fleet. On Tuesday, Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the bridge, forcing its main road arch to crumble into the sea while leaving a yawning gap, according to videos and images verified by Reuters.
This week's first attack, on Monday, caused more minor damage, but gave Ukrainian forces a chance to see how Russian air defences would react.

items.summary: Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for the use of blood booster EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday, adding that she admitted to ...
items.body:
Athletics-World marathon champion Jepchirchir banned for three years over EPO use Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for the use of blood booster EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday, adding that she admitted to breaching anti-doping rules.
Reuters | Updated: 19-11-2026 12:43 IST | Created: 19-11-2026 12:43 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways
AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for the use of blood booster EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Thursday, adding that she admitted to breaching anti-doping rules.
One of the most decorated women in the sport, the 33-year-old has won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and claimed major marathon victories in New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney. The breaches related to the "presence of a prohibited substance or its metabolites or markers in an athlete's sample" and the "use or attempted use by an athlete of a prohibited substance or a prohibited method", the AIU said.
Jepchirchir was given a provisional suspension last month, after testing positive for the banned substance in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory in August. The AIU said the sample returned an adverse analytical finding (AAF) on September 17.
"In an interview on that same date, the athlete denied using EPO and said she had no knowledge of how the AAF had occurred," the AIU added. "Despite her explanations in the interview, the former world record-holder in the half-marathon subsequently signed an admission of anti-doping rule violations and acceptance of consequences form," it added.
In the form, she accepted disqualification of all her competitive results since 17 July 2026, including her victory in the Sydney Marathon, it said. On Thursday, Sydney marathon authorities said Irine Cheptai would be crowned the 2026 women's champion after Jepchirchir's disqualification.

Anthropic clinches biggest IPO ever with US$81 billion offering

Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion.

People visit an Anthropic booth at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, on Sep 17, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Carlos Barria)

FAST

Anthropic's IPO raised US$81.31 billion on Wednesday (Nov 18), eclipsing SpaceX’s offering to claim the title of the largest stock-market debut on record.
Anthropic said the IPO was priced at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range and valuing the company at approximately US$1.5 trillion.
Reuters was first to report that the IPO was upsized by about 19 per cent to 980 million shares from its initial plan to sell 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece. 
Anthropic is also raising US$26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price, the filings show.

On a fully diluted basis, the IPO values the company at about US$1.5 trillion, including securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, the valuation stands at about US$1.1 trillion.
Anthropic, the first major frontier artificial-intelligence model developer to do an IPO, follows SpaceX's June offering, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating AI models.

Also read:

Commentary: Anthropic’s mega IPO is coming. Don’t let hype drive your investment decisions

CNA Explains: Why AI leaders are calling for a slowdown – and what makes it so difficult

CHALLENGING BACKDROP FOR AI STOCKS The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX's record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging. 
Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry's growth.
The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company's outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies.
The company's closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year.
Anthropic's growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers. 
Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing.
The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

Also read:

Commentary: Anthropic’s call for AI development pause deserves attention. It also raises questions

Commentary: Some Anthropic engineers think AI might end us. Why race ahead?

SPENDING COMMITMENTS EXPOSE RISKS But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier. 
It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.
Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion from the second quarter. 
The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the previous quarter. 
The net loss narrowed to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating items related to bonds convertible into its shares.
Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models.
Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances. Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity.
"If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered," Anthropic said in an IPO filing.
Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fueled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-centre operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities.
Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety. 
CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society's ability to manage the risks.

Also read:

Singapore backs international call for greater frontier AI safeguards

Existing safeguards by AI companies insufficient as models grow more capable: Josephine Teo

COMPETITION AND SAFETY CHALLENGES Competition is intensifying against Anthropic to be the leading provider of AI tools for businesses.
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, its latest flagship AI model, accounted for about 13 per cent of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with about 8 per cent for Anthropic's Claude Fable, according to data cited by Reuters in September. 
OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate also passed US$40 billion in July, although Anthropic maintained a lead at the time.
The competitive threat extends beyond the handful of companies developing the most powerful commercial models. More large companies are looking to adopt these models, which can be downloaded and run independently, to rein in AI spending.
A recent Capgemini study found that 59 per cent of executives at large companies plan to increase their use of open-weight models over the next year as AI costs exceed budgets.
Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic's largest customers, has been looking to reduce its use of the startup's models as it develops more AI capabilities internally, Reuters previously reported.
"There's going to be other models out there ... Our thesis is that the vast amount of value will accrue to whoever is at the frontier," said Peter Singlehurst, head of private companies at Baillie Gifford, which invested roughly US$1.5 billion in Anthropic before its IPO. 
"Our bet is that Anthropic has the ingredients - that doesn't guarantee, but means that they arguably have the highest probability of remaining at the frontier."
Anthropic's IPO prospectus warned that its models could develop capabilities faster than the company could evaluate them and put adequate safeguards in place.
"Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm," Anthropic said in the filing.
The company has said it is considering tighter human oversight of some research and development decisions as its AI models take on a growing share of that work.
Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic's offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate. 
The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX's IPO earlier this year.

Source: Reuters/rl

items.title: U.S. futures point higher led by rebound for Nvidia
items.author: The Associated Press
items.summary: Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher Wednesday after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang.
items.body: NEW YORK — A fifth straight drop for the S&P 500 on Wednesday dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, as Nvidia and other stocks tied to artificial intelligence technology kept swinging on uncertainty about how much strength is left in the AI boom. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561 points, or 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. Nvidia once again was at the centre of the market’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected. But the stock quickly erased all its gain and then finished with a loss of 2.9 per cent. The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself. “Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia, though, failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory chips exploded with the AI boom, went from an early rise of 1.5 per cent to a drop of 1 per cent. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents access to them out to customers over the cloud, sank 4.1 per cent and has lost nearly a third of its value so far this year. The entire industry has been swinging recently. Besides criticism that AI stock prices simply shot too high in their frenzy, the industry is facing worries that this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections could mean more regulation for it. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of oil companies were heavy weights due to drops for oil prices. ExxonMobil fell four per cent, and Chevron sank 4 per cent after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.3 per cent to settle at US$91.95. The drop in oil prices helped to pull yields down in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 5.06 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Tuesday. High yields have made mortgages more expensive to get, which has chilled the housing industry. But they’ve moderated over the last month, and a report on Wednesday said homebuilders broke ground on more projects last month than economists expected. That helped push stocks of homebuilders modestly higher, and Lennar added 0.7 per cent. Some of the strongest gains on Wall Street came from retailers following their profit reports. TJX rallied 8 per cent after the company behind the TJ Maxx and Marshalls stores reported slightly better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Ernie Herrman said he expects momentum to accelerate through the holiday shopping season. Target climbed four per cent following a better-than-expected profit report, which included its strongest quarterly sales gain in roughly five years. Take-Two Interactive Software revved 6.2 per cent higher amid glowing reviews for its latest “Grand Theft Auto” video game. All told, the S&P 500 fell 16.90 points to 7,323.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 to 50,198.17, and the Nasdaq composite rose 101.50 to 24,429.88. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 sank 1.3 per cent after a report said inflation in the United Kingdom worsened. That could up the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates to get inflation under control. Expectations are high that the Federal Reserve in Washington will raise its own interest rate when it meets next month, after it made no move last month. Notes released Wednesday from the Fed’s latest meeting indicated some officials are considering a larger increase to rates than usual in December. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2 per cent a day after dropping to its lowest closing level since February. It’s swung in particular because its market is dominated by two stocks tied to the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report.

ANTALYA: Efforts to boost electrification will depend on fossil fuels , OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said on Wednesday (Nov 18) at the COP31 talks , where host Türkiye is seeking to make increased electricity use a central outcome of the conference.
Türkiye has presented a target to increase electricity's share of final energy demand worldwide to 35 per cent by 2035 from around 20 per cent now as a way to curb climate change driven by carbon emissions.
But it has not specified that the extra power needs to be carbon-free, which critics say greatly weakens any impact it might have on tackling climate change.
Al Ghais also said electrification was not a panacea.

"While electrification is a core part of our energy future, let us also remember that it is also heavily dependent on oil. Grid expansion requires more petroleum-derived products and diesel-powered heavy machinery," he said in a speech delivered in the venue's plenary hall.
"While undoubtedly important, electrification is not the only solution to the world's environmental challenges."
Al Ghais said increased electrification came with risks, including cyberattacks on energy systems and possible issues with the s up ply of critical minerals.
"We will require all energies for energy security. We will require all energies to achieve sustainable development goals. We will require all energies to accommodate differences in national circumstances," he said.

Related:

Nations haggle over draft climate deal at UN talks

World leaders set out clashing priorities as COP31 turns to negotiations

The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies, a gro up ing known as OPEC +, has previously caused up set at UN climate talks by backing the continued use of fossil fuels .
At COP28 in Dubai, for instance, it called on member countries of OPEC + to reject proposals for any text under negotiation that targeted curbing the use of fossil fuels as opposed to emissions. That conference agreed language on shifting away from fossil fuels , but did not commit to phasing them out.
Türkiye's own energy system relies on fossil fuels .
The hosts said on Wednesday that so far 75 of the nearly 200 countries attending the talks in the Mediterranean city of Antalya have backed the voluntary pledge.
The talks are scheduled to end on Friday, but, judging by previous COP meetings, they could go on longer if a deal has not been finalised.

Source: Reuters/fs

FAST

Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products.
Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent.
Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi.
The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.

"As AI accelerates cyber attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms," Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said during the company's analyst call on Wednesday.
With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.
Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors.
"Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen.
The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion.
Its first-quarter revenue came in at $3.45 billion, up 39 per cent from a year earlier, beating estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

items.title: Alberta government to require cleanup funds to be set aside for each new well drilled
items.author: The Canadian Press
items.summary: The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled.
items.body: The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled. If passed, the bill would create the Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund. Money would follow each well through its life cycle, even if ownership changes hands. Companies would be required to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The new rules are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027. Between the payments and compound interest that accrues over time, there should be enough money available to fund the eventual cleanup of a typical well, Brian Jean, minister of energy and minerals, told a news conference Wednesday. “We are making sure that when these wells are drilled, we have something set aside for them to be cleaned up so that the taxpayers are not on the hook.” Managing the backlog of old oil and gas wells that have no one legally responsible for them, due to bankruptcy and other factors, has been a long-running issue in Alberta. Farmers have raised concern about contamination from inactive wells on their land. Cleanup of such sites is managed through the non-profit Orphan Well Association and is funded through an industry fee, the amount of which the Alberta Energy Regulator recommends to the Alberta government every year. That fee would continue to exist. The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion. The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells are waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe. Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state. In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700. Under the new rules — proposed as part of a broader bill that also includes new restrictions for data centres, greater illegal dumping fines and other matters — a company would be eligible to receive the funds that were set aside once reclamation is complete. If the well becomes orphaned, the funding would be transferred to the Orphan Well Association. “We’re making good on a promise that we made to Albertans to stop the flow of unfunded wells to the Orphan Well Association,” Jean said. “After these changes are put into effect, no new oil and gas well will end up at the OWA without industry-paid-for closure funding.” Terry Schmidtke, who chairs the Alberta Small Producers Group, said the changes will give junior oil and gas companies greater confidence to buy and sell producing wells that are drilled after the rules take effect. “By ensuring cleanup funding stays with each well when ownership changes, smaller producers can continue to invest and grow while meeting their long-term cleanup obligations and keeping Albertans employed in the industry right across the province,” Schmidtke said in the province’s news release. Farmers have long demanded greater assurances that oil and gas sites on their land will be properly cleaned up, Peter Dobbie, a property rights advocate, said in the provincial release. “These changes should ensure that any new wells drilled will be cleaned up and returned to full agricultural use when they stop producing.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026. Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

Anthropic IPO to mint thousands of millionaires

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Anthropic's initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history.  
The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world's most valuable companies.
The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely.
Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $100 million in equity after the initial public offering, which is slated to open on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $83 a share, above its initial target range that would value the company at up to $1.4 trillion, according to a person familiar with the information.

Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2,800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $1 million of pretax vested equity at a $1.35 trillion valuation, the middle of the price range. 
The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals.
But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast.  Anthropic option holders were sitting on $119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately. 
Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates.
"The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for," Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. "It doesn't get better than this."
EQUITY AT ENTRY LEVEL
Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago —  even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $1. 
Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows. 
At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went  public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade.   
"Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO," Benson said, referring to Anthropic.
Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings.
EARLY HIRES REAP REWARDS
Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5,300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool.
A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic's stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers. 
The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $140,000 to $190,000. 
The posting added that equity would be "a major component of the total compensation" beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay.
That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $1.30 per share.
"And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organization chart do quite well in IPO," said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra.
Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes.
Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead.
After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said.

Source: Reuters

items.title: Carney striking trade deals at ‘lightning speed’ amid diversification push: expert
items.author: Jordan Fleguel
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is moving fast to secure new trade deals as his government attempts to make Canada less dependent on the U.S., but there’s reason to be optimistic that an agreement between ...
items.body: Prime Minister Mark Carney is moving fast to secure new trade deals as his government attempts to make Canada less dependent on the U.S., but there’s reason to be optimistic that an agreement between Ottawa and Washington could come soon, an expert says. “Canada has successfully concluded several free trade agreements with our Association of Southeast Asian Nations counterparts and with the Philippines at kind of a lightning speed,” Margaret Kim, international trade counsel at Gowling WLG, told BNN Bloomberg Wednesday. “These are all part of Canada’s efforts to diversify trade away from the United States given the increasing complexity of our trade relations.” Kim’s comments came on the same day Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, where the two leaders “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement,” according to a post-meeting readout. While trade negotiations with the U.S. remain top of mind for Carney’s government, he’s also been focused on building Canada’s economic relationship with China, the world’s second largest economy. Carney’s trip began with an announcement that Canada would drop some restrictions on imports of Chinese steel and aluminum in exchange for greater market access for Canadian pork, seafood and other agricultural products. “I think overall the tariff relief is a positive development for sure, especially for those in the pork and seafood industry,” said Kim. “We will see how this renewed sense of economic co-operation between Canada and China further develops… from a legal perspective we have to be mindful that these are provisional arrangements short of a full-fledged free trade agreement, which would give us and businesses more certainty.” Kim said Canada and China have signalled that “this is the first of many further discussions to be had,” which will likely include talks related to the sale of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) in Canada. “I think in the area of EVs, certainly China is interested in bringing more China-manufactured EVs into the Canadian market,” she said. “But from the Canadian perspective, I think prime minister Carney has clearly stated that it has to be within the terms that are acceptable within the realities of the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).” ‘Stay optimistic’ The future of CUSMA and the broader trading relationship between Canada and the U.S. remains uncertain, as the two neighbours have yet to strike a new deal that would end a monthslong trade war. Kim said despite the diplomatic tensions and industry-specific tariffs and counter tariffs currently in place, she doesn’t see CUSMA “going anywhere,” but added that “certainly, there will be different versions of it.” Much of the negotiations between the Carney and Trump governments have taken place behind the scenes, Kim noted, saying that the two leaders meeting face to face on Wednesday is a good sign. “I think we have to stay optimistic,” she said, “and see how it shakes out.” With files from CTV News’ Graham Richardson and The Canadian Press

items.title: Indonesian miners scramble for clarity as Prabowo seeks greater state share
items.author: Mining.com
items.creator: Mining.com
items.summary: Miners in Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, nickel and tin, are scrambling to decipher President Prabowo Subianto’s call for the st
items.body: Miners in Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, nickel and tin, are scrambling to decipher President Prabowo Subianto’s call for the state to secure greater benefits from mining operations, warning that the uncertainty could deter investment in the resource-rich nation. The comments add to concerns among investors over policy uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy – home to the world’s largest gold mine and the biggest known nickel reserves – which has already been rattled by warnings from international credit ratings agencies and the prospect of MSCI excluding the country from its stock market indexes. Indonesia’s energy stock index .JKENERGY, which includes shares of coal miners, has dropped 4.1% since Prabowo’s weekend comments – while the basic materials stock index .JKBASIC, which covers miners of other minerals, has lost 6.2%. Prabowo, speaking on Saturday, said he had instructed ministers to ensure the state receives at least “70% of the benefits from all mining permits” and added that, if necessary, the state should “take over stakes” in companies in Indonesia. The president did not spell out what constituted “benefits” or how the 70% would be calculated, leaving miners and analysts trying to assess whether he was referring to profits, revenue, taxes and royalties, or a broader measure of the state’s economic benefit. “We are still examining what President Prabowo meant by his intention for 70% of mining sector proceeds to go into state coffers,” Sudirman Widhy Hartono, chairman of the Association of Mining Professionals, told Reuters. He said the industry was awaiting a more detailed explanation from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. The ministry did not respond to a request from Reuters for comment. A spokesperson for the president did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The mining sector, especially in nickel and coal, is already struggling with tighter production quotas and rising costs. French miner Eramet, which was forced to halt operations for several months due to a lower mining quota, is planning to sell some stake in its Indonesian nickel mine. “The mere uncertainty surrounding definitions is enough to delay new investment decisions,” said Fauzan Luthfi Djamal, mining analyst with brokerage Mirae Asset Sekuritas Indonesia. “Foreign partners involved in nickel downstreaming are likely re-evaluating project returns, while financing costs could potentially rise.” Mineral-rich Indonesia had seen massive investment in its nickel processing sector following a raw nickel export ban in 2020, and a similar ban on other minerals in 2023. Impact on companies Fauzan said the state’s objective of increasing revenue from natural resources is “understandable” but the challenge is designing a scheme that captures windfall gains without stifling business or deterring new investment. Sudirman said data from coal mining companies showed total state revenue can reach around 32% of total sales, while companies earn profits of less than 10% – which means government revenue is more than three times company profit. Depending on how the 70% “benefit” is calculated, Fauzan estimated net profits for privately owned miners could be cut by as much as half, while mines operating under special mining licences could see profits fall by up to a third. Fauzan said the quickest route would probably be through higher royalties, with the government having previously considered increases for gold, copper, silver, nickel and tin. Other possibilities include additional levies or requiring state equity participation when mining licences are extended or converted. Indonesia had earlier this year shelved plans to impose windfall taxes on coal and nickel exports and increase royalties on some mining companies. In May, Prabowo said exports of coal, palm oil and ferroalloys would be controlled by state-run Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia to combat exports being under-invoiced. The proposal was subsequently scaled back, with the agency saying its initial role would be as a centralised data collector. In August, Prabowo also announced a commodities exchange and said Indonesia should set its own prices rather than follow global benchmarks. “Prabowo often issues directives,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, an economist at the Center of Economics and Law Studies think tank. “Yet the technical regulations are never prepared beforehand … we’re seeing this happen again.” (Reporting by Fransiska Nangoy and Bernadette Christina; Writing by Gibran Peshimam; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

Nov 18 : Millions of gamers around the world have logged on for the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," arguably the century's most anticipated video game, offering a glimpse of the vast, interconnected digital infrastructure the global economy increasingly relies on.
No major disruption is expected from the rollout. But the scale of demand around one of the gaming industry's biggest releases underscores a broader risk for insurers: a failure at a shared cloud, payments or technology provider could affect thousands of businesses at once.
After 13 years in development and an estimated $1 billion or more in production costs, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' began rolling out globally on Thursday, drawing the kind of attention that few entertainment releases ever command.
But the fervour also underscores how much modern businesses depend on the digital infrastructure that makes such mass online activity possible, and the risks insurers face when that infrastructure fails.

"A launch of the scale of GTA VI is effectively a built-in stress test of the shared digital economy infrastructure," said Marcos Alvarez, managing director at Morningstar DBRS.
Insurers cover businesses against financial losses stemming from disruptions to their operations, including some caused by technology failures.
As companies increasingly rely on the same cloud providers, payment systems and digital platforms, a single outage could trigger claims from multiple policyholders at once, amplifying exposure.
Despite the frenzy surrounding the launch, any disruption on launch day or in the days that follow would not necessarily spell disaster for insurers, industry experts said.
"The recent technology outages have been a case in point with the gap between the economic cost and the actual insured loss being quite large due to policy limits, retentions, waiting periods, and coverage exclusions," Alvarez added.
Business interruption could be a major source of claims, but coverage could also extend to costs associated with data recovery, system restoration, cyberattacks and outages at third-party technology providers, depending on the policy.
"This is an area that is evolving rapidly for the insurance industry. Insurers are refining how they assess, model and manage these interconnected exposures," said Loretta Worters, a spokesperson for the Insurance Information Institute.
"That means looking beyond an individual company's cybersecurity protections to understand its reliance on third-party providers, the concentration of those dependencies across their portfolios and the potential for a single event to generate losses across multiple policyholders."

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Texas has resumed issuing air permits for data centers, state regulators said on Wednesday, after pausing the practice last month as part of the state's broader attempt to manage the server warehouses and their effects on the electrical grid, communities and the environment.
• The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said.
• Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted the connection of new data centers to the state electric grid in August and ordered an audit of the projects, rattling one of the world's fastest-growing hubs for data center development. Abbott followed up by temporarily blocking air permits for all data center projects.
• The air permit resumption came after the Texas grid operator notified the TCEQ that it had collected "community impact review" information for proposed data center projects, Lopez said.

FAST

PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 18 : An Abu Dhabi court has ordered several major cryptocurrency companies to freeze digital assets worth billions of dollars as part of efforts to recover some of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen from wallets operated by Binance, according to court documents seen by Reuters.
The Abu Dhabi Global Market Court decision seeks to prevent the stolen crypto from being moved and applies to companies including Circle and World Liberty Financial.
The court said the 18 named companies were not accused of wrongdoing. Many companies have already frozen tokens that were stolen from Binance on October 29 in the largest crypto heist on record. US authorities have attributed the attack to North Korea.
“We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers,” Dugan Bliss, deputy general counsel at Binance, said in a statement on Wednesday.

The Abu Dhabi Global Market financial center serves as Binance's global hub, and the company said the Financial Services Regulatory Authority there is its primary regulator.
Reuters was the first to report that Binance was granted a court order to aid asset recovery. Binance subsequently said in a blog post on Wednesday that, while it had absorbed the financial impact of the stolen funds and made customers whole, it had a responsibility to pursue the stolen assets and support law enforcement. 
BILLIONS ALREADY FROZEN
Binance has previously said that around $2.85 billion worth of the stolen crypto tokens had been frozen or intercepted by third parties. That includes Circle, which operates the stablecoin USDC, and World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture operated by US President Donald Trump's family, which has a stablecoin called USD1. Both tokens are pegged to the US dollar. 
Under the court order, those firms and 16 others are required to maintain the freeze on the tokens involved in the heist, pending further court proceedings. They are also barred from lending, swapping or mixing the tokens with other assets. 
El Salvador-based Tether, which issues the USDT token and previously said it had frozen $1.5 billion worth of the stolen funds, was not included in the court order. Bliss said Binance was working with Tether directly on the return of the frozen assets.
"In consultation with the relevant authorities, we will work directly with Binance in respect of reissuing the tokens," a spokesperson for Tether said.
Binance has hired US law firm Gibson Dunn as part of its efforts to recover the stolen crypto. In a statement, a lawyer from Gibson Dunn representing Binance called the injunction "one of, if not the, largest publicly known freezing orders ever made."
FURTHER HEARING SCHEDULED
A further hearing is scheduled for December 1, when the court will consider whether the proprietary injunction — a freezing order that applies to claimed assets — should continue and on what terms. 
David Wachsman, spokesman for World Liberty Financial, said: "As the security incident unfolded in real time, World Liberty received an alert from onchain data identifying the issue. We acted decisively to protect our users and our partners."
In a statement, a spokesperson for Circle said the company continues to coordinate with Binance and law enforcement, adding that Circle does not comment on specific legal proceedings.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Options on Anthropic shares could begin trading as soon as Monday, giving investors a new way to wager on the AI company's prospects as market participants expect heavy interest.
Cboe Global Markets expects to list the contracts two business days after the stock begins trading, pending industry readiness. “The Anthropic IPO could be yet another catalyst, bringing a new wave of investors and trading activity to the options market," said Rob Hocking, Cboe’s global head of derivatives. "It’s great to see investor education driving this growth, as more people learn how options let them define their risk. An exciting trend and one we expect to continue.” 
The Claude developer is expected to price its IPO later on Wednesday, and the shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.  
"We expect significant interest in Anthropic options once they list," said Garrett DeSimone, head quant at OptionMetrics. "The combination of AI-driven enthusiasm and the lottery-like payoff profile typical of IPOs are likely to draw investors immediately. As one of the most concentrated pure-play exposures to AI, the stock is also likely to be highly volatile."

"The AI trade is melting down," Gottlieb said. "Many feel it is overdone, while many others feel it's the popping of a bubble. Whenever there is such opposing views in a heated market, we get a lot of option positioning."
Options give holders the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell shares at a set price within a certain period. They offer investors a cheaper way to gain exposure to a stock and to express their views on both short-term price moves and longer-term positioning.
Anthropic’s $64 billion IPO has drawn stronger early institutional demand than the offering of SpaceX, with the book six times oversubscribed last week, Reuters previously reported.
The IPO has drawn anticipation from investors, with Wall Street rolling out products tied to the stock, hosting client events and giving away merchandise ahead of the AI company's potentially record launch.

FAST

Nov 18 : While the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, "creating short-term disruption in the way the system works."
Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a program or product.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats Wednesday that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related. But Clayton said the speed and level of capability of computer systems are "increasing substantially," so legacy computer systems and equipment that already were old are aging much more quickly.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.
At least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a source at the bank said, speaking on condition of anonymity. 
"AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it," said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security. 
"Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure," Itzchakov said.
Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world. 
"Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical," Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. "Not all vulnerabilities are created equal."
Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponize vulnerabilities, but is a more "valuable friend" to those tasked with defending key computer networks.
"AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities," said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former President Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. "And when patching at scale, some can cause problems."
Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking "incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating I don't believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money." 
"Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen," Gestiehr said. "What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers."

Source: Reuters

items.title: Copper price craters as AI, tariff trades unwind, wiping $186 billion off top producers in a month
items.author: Frik Els
items.creator: Staff Writer
items.summary: Stan Druckenmiller has gone short and Asia Copper Week heard that demand is ‘recessionary-like’, yet Chinese buyers are paying a record premium for prompt metal.
items.body:
Copper price craters as AI, tariff trades unwind, wiping $186 billion off top producers in a month
Stan Druckenmiller has gone short and Asia Copper Week heard that demand is ‘recessionary-like’, yet Chinese buyers are paying a record premium for prompt metal.

Staff Writer
|
November 18, 2026 - 8:58 am

Categories:
Markets

Credit: Adobe Stock

Copper plunged to its lowest since April on Wednesday as speculators abandoned bets tied to the artificial intelligence boom, a surging dollar and fading US tariff prospects overwhelmed signs of acute physical shortage in China, and the loss of key chart levels added to momentum selling, dragging shares of the biggest producers down by between 5% and 9%.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, fell as much as 6.7% to $5.5835 a pound ($12,309 a tonne) in late morning trade, the lowest since early April, and more than 82,000 contracts had changed hands by midday. The contract has fallen for five sessions in a row and at the day’s low was down 16% in three weeks and 19% below the record settlement of $6.8885 reached on September 9. A gain for 2026 that stood at 22% at the peak has been wiped out, with the price dipping below where it ended last year.

On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper was down 3.4% at $12,772.50 a tonne in official trading and later extended its loss to as much as 5.6%, the lowest since April, Bloomberg reports. In Shanghai the most-traded contract shed 3.4% to 97,920 yuan ($14,690) a tonne, and tin, the other metal most closely tied to AI hardware, slumped more than 7% in London to its lowest in almost eight months.

Underlying consumption is not helping either. “Copper demand today is closer to a recessionary-like environment than growth environment,” Nicholas Snowdon, head of metals and mining research at Mercuria, told the World Copper Conference Asia in Shanghai on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg. Natixis analysts have described the combination of US stockpiling and AI-linked investment flows as a bubble, while banks remain split on whether 2027 brings shortage or surplus .

Miners routed

The selling spread to equities as the session wore on. Eleven of the largest copper-exposed miners lost a combined $49 billion, or more than 6% of their market value, by early afternoon in New York, taking their losses to $112 billion over the past week and $186 billion, or 20%, over the past month.

BHP dropped 6.5% to a market value of $178 billion, $32 billion less than a month ago and well under the $207 billion it was worth during last week’s short-lived bounce . Southern Copper has been hit hardest among the majors, down 5.2% on the day and 26% in a month to $125 billion, a loss of $45 billion that has cut its 2026 gain to 6% from 41% in mid-October. Freeport-McMoRan, worth about $100 billion a month ago, fell 6.7% to $74 billion and is barely positive for the year.

Rio Tinto lost 5.1% to $130 billion and Glencore 6.5% to $72 billion, while Anglo American fell 8.0% and Teck Resources 7.4%. Antofagasta and Lundin Mining were the day’s worst performers among the larger names, both down more than 9%, and along with Rio are now in negative territory for 2026.

First Quantum Minerals, which jumped on Tuesday after Panama opened formal talks on restarting Cobre Panama , fell 5.5% and is 23% lower over the month. Ivanhoe Mines has shed 34% in a month and 58% in 2026.

Towel thrown in

Investors appear to be giving up after the loss of several technical levels added to momentum selling, Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank, told Reuters, pointing to an inflation scare and the risk of higher funding costs. “AI was a trigger, but it’s not really the driver,” he said.

Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities, described the move to Bloomberg as a complete recalibration of the copper market: worries about Federal Reserve tightening are weighing on the demand outlook, the midterm results have dented optimism about AI spending, and the New York premium over London, a proxy for tariff expectations, is narrowing. Speculative positioning has largely unwound and in places flipped net short, while selling by trend-following funds has accelerated the decline, McKay said.

Tech stocks steadied on Wednesday after Nvidia reported a 103% jump in quarterly revenue to $115.8 billion late on Tuesday, the chipmaker’s first results since Jensen Huang’s exit rattled the metals demand story , but that did nothing for copper. The dollar is holding near a 19-month high ahead of the release of minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October meeting, at which two officials voted for another rate increase.

Sentiment took a further knock late on Tuesday when Stan Druckenmiller, among the best-known backers of copper’s AI trade, told a conference in Austin he is now short the metal. A filing earlier in the week showed his family office had sold out of Southern Copper and bought gold miners during the third quarter.

Druckenmiller exits copper, steel and chip stocks to buy gold miners

Fund positioning has already been cut hard. Managed money net long positions on Comex have fallen from more than 80,000 contracts six weeks ago to about 35,000, close to a 14-month low, according to Saxo. Hansen put the next chart supports at $5.63 and $5.32 a pound. The first of those, which is also where copper ended 2025, gave way later in the session.

Record premium, falling price

The rout comes with the physical market in China as tight as it has been in years. The Yangshan premium paid to import copper into the country jumped by about a fifth to a record $360 a tonne on Wednesday, Reuters reports, up from less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks dropped 18% last week to 27,642 tonnes, the lowest since December 2023, and the November contract expired on Monday at a premium of more than $2,000 a tonne to December, a squeeze that forced the exchange to intervene .

Investors increasingly doubt the Trump administration will press ahead with tariffs on refined copper after this month’s midterm elections, and the spike in Chinese prices has created the commercial case for traders to ship metal out of the United States, where warehouses hold roughly 85% of the 1.09 million tonnes in exchange-monitored stocks. The assumption that those inventories would stay stranded unless tariffs were formally ruled out has been shaken, Bloomberg reports.

Supply news ignored

Chile’s copper commission Cochilco expects national output to fall 8.4% this year to 4.94 million tonnes, the lowest in 23 years , after production dropped 8.5% to 3.63 million tonnes in the first nine months. The country’s leaching operations are also exposed to sulphuric acid supply: imports hit a record 3.97 million tonnes last year, about half of consumption, and China supplied 37% of that before restricting exports in May.

In Shanghai, where the industry has gathered for annual supply talks, China’s Nonferrous Metals Industry Association said concentrate-fed smelting capacity has nearly reached a ceiling and promised a monitoring mechanism to bring treatment charges back to sustainable levels. Spot charges sank to a record minus $247.20 a tonne on November 6, meaning smelters pay miners for the privilege of processing their concentrate.

The 2026 benchmark was set at zero, and 21 of 35 industry participants polled by Reuters expect a negative number for 2027, with forecasts from minus $50 to minus $150. Snowdon argued that the more negative the benchmark, the healthier the market in the long run. Freeport Indonesia is meanwhile offering 2027 cathode from its Manyar smelter to Chinese buyers at a premium of $158 a tonne, Reuters reports, citing two sources.

The MINING.COM TOP 50 ranking of the world’s most valuable miners had already lost $226 billion in October.

Stocks slip with eyes on Anthropic and Nvidia, oil prices slide

FAST

NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 18 : A gauge of stocks across the globe fell on Wednesday after Nvidia's quarterly results and ahead of Anthropic's market debut, while the dollar's strength on the back of a hawkish Federal Reserve weighed on trader sentiment.
The dollar index strengthened to a fresh 19-month high after US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the central bank needs to either approve a half-point interest rate hike at its December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027.
Mining stocks dragged European shares lower, while Nvidia's results initially helped Asian shares, with South Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight. But the Nvidia rally fizzled and its stock fell 2.9 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent.
Nvidia's board dismissed the idea of rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week. The company's results and strong outlook did not dispel uncertainty.

"We believe (Tuesday's) results have stabilized sentiment and put a floor under the recent AI selloff, but they have postponed rather than permanently cured investor anxiety," said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.11 per cent to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 0.23 per cent to 7,323.63 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42 per cent to 24,429.89. 
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 0.45 per cent to 1,074.61.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 1.03 per cent, while emerging market stocks fell 0.2 per cent. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.28 per cent to 59,024.28.
The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares its market debut on Thursday. The company priced its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above the expected range, according to a person familiar with the matter.
DOLLAR UP, OIL DOWN
In currencies, the dollar strengthened as Waller's comments and recent economic data cemented expectations for an interest rate hike next month.
"The Federal Reserve seems at the moment to be very determined to hike interest rates and maybe even aggressively do so," said Juan Perez, senior director of trading at Monex USA in Washington. "That's the belief right now that's carrying the US dollar."
The dollar index rose 0.17 per cent to 103.79, with the euro down 0.22 per cent at $1.0973.
In commodities markets, crude prices fell after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, adding to expectations of a supply surplus. 
US crude lost 3.3 per cent to $83.17 a barrel and Brent fell to $91.84 per barrel, down 1.4 per cent.
Spot gold dropped 3.24 per cent to $3,725.10 an ounce and spot silver fell 4.98 per cent to $45.04 an ounce. Copper declined 4.54 per cent to $12,626.00 a ton.
Yields on 2-year US Treasury notes, which are sensitive to interest rate expectations, edged higher on hawkish Fed speaker comments and minutes from the last monetary policy committee meeting that underscored inflation worries.
The 2-year note yield rose 1.31 basis points to 4.802 per cent, from 4.789 per cent late on Tuesday, while the benchmark US 10-year note yield fell 3.47 basis points to 5.068 per cent, from 5.103 per cent.

Source: Reuters

items.title: Brazil pushes back on EU review of Anglo American nickel deal
items.author: Cecilia Jamasmie
items.creator: Staff Writer
items.summary: Brazil disputes Brussels' authority over a Chinese acquisition as Anglo American warns its two nickel mines could close.
items.body:
Brazil pushes back on EU review of Anglo American nickel deal
Brazil disputes Brussels' authority over a Chinese acquisition as Anglo American warns its two nickel mines could close.

Staff Writer
|
November 18, 2026 - 3:43 am

Categories:
Critical Minerals
Top Companies

Barro Alto. ( Image courtesy of Anglo American | Flickr. )

Brazil has challenged the European Union’s scrutiny of Anglo American’s (LON: AAL) $500-million sale of its Brazilian nickel operations to China’s MMG (HKE: 1208), raising concerns about foreign regulators intervening in domestic mining transactions.

Brazil’s foreign ministry wrote to the European Commission, the EU’s antitrust regulator, arguing that the deal involves Brazilian assets and falls outside its jurisdiction, Reuters reported. The Commission is reviewing whether MMG could redirect ferronickel supplies from Europe to China, potentially hurting European stainless steel producers.

“If the transaction is prohibited, Anglo American will place Barro Alto and Codemin (mines) into care and maintenance, with closure as the objective. This is not a negotiating position,” Anglo American CEO Duncan Wanblad wrote last week to executives at ferronickel customers including Acerinox (BME: ACX), Aperam (AMS: APAM) and Outokumpu (HEL: OUT1V).

The dispute highlights growing tensions between national control over critical minerals and foreign competition oversight, as governments seek to protect strategic resources and industrial supply chains. Brazil has identified nickel as a priority mineral because of its economic and geopolitical importance, while European authorities are seeking to safeguard supplies for domestic manufacturers.

Sovereignty concerns

Brazil’s competition regulator, Cade, has not opposed the transaction. A European Commission spokesperson confirmed contact with Brazilian authorities but declined further comment.

Brazilian mining industry association Ibram has joined the EU investigation as an interested third party. Its head of institutional affairs, Pablo Cesario, warned that the review could set a precedent for foreign intervention in transactions involving Brazilian assets.

EU scrutiny of Anglo-MMG nickel deal tests China stance

The challenge comes as Brazil strengthens oversight of its mineral sector. The country’s newly established National Council for the Industrialization of Critical and Strategic Minerals has placed nickel among its priorities, reflecting efforts to retain greater influence over resources important to industrial development.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva had planned to raise the dispute with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at a climate conference in Turkey, but the meeting did not take place.

Supply risks

MMG has offered assurances that ferronickel deliveries to European customers would continue after the acquisition, seeking to address concerns about potential supply disruptions.

The proposed takeover puts Anglo American’s efforts to divest its Brazilian nickel assets at odds with European competition concerns, leaving the future of the operations dependent on regulatory approval.

The European Commission is scheduled to decide on the transaction by Dec. 21.

(With files from Reuters)

items.title: テンセントがオラクルからAI半導体10万個をリース、70億ドル規模－FT
items.author: Bloomberg
items.creator: Bloomberg
items.summary:
（ブルームバーグ）： 中国のテンセント・ホールディングス（騰訊）は、東南アジアでオラクルから先端のAI半導体を借り受けることで合意した。テンセントにとってAI半導体のリース契約としては過去最大規模となる。英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（FT）が事情に詳しい関係者の話として報じた。

報道によると、テンセントは、5年間の契約の一環として10万個の半導体を利用できるようになる。契約額は70億ドル（約1兆1000億円）に上るという。

中国のAI開発企業は米国の輸出規制を回避するため、米エヌビディア製など中国国内では入手できないAIアクセラレーターを海外で借りて利用している。中国のテクノロジー企業は、東南アジアのデータセンターの最大顧客層の一つとなっている。

テンセントとオラクルの担当者は、ブルームバーグ・ニュースのコメント要請に直ちに応じなかった。

原題：Tencent Leases AI Chips From Oracle
